opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core intuition is that when you only train a small model on the teacher's sampled outputs, the final tokens it actually chose, you're throwing away a huge amount of information. Each token the teacher emits is really one sample from a full distribution over the vocabulary, and that distribution carries what people call "dark knowledge." It tells you which alternatives the teacher thought were plausible, how confident it was, and where it was uncertain. With logits distillation the student sees that whole distribution at every position, so you get many more bits of supervision per token than a one-hot label gives you.

For reasoning in particular I think this matters even more. Reasoning traces have these critical forking points: a step where the model could try one approach or another, or a token where it decides whether to double-check or move on. If you train on hard samples alone, the student just copies whatever branch the teacher happened to take. With the full distribution, it learns that there were several reasonable continuations and roughly how to weigh them. That's a much richer signal about the teacher's actual policy, not just one trajectory out of it.

There's also an efficiency angle. Small models are capacity-limited, so you want every training token to count. Dense supervision from logits tends to be far more sample-efficient than SFT on generated traces, so you can get much closer to the teacher on the same compute budget.

And the piece I'm most excited about is combining it with on-policy training, which is what we explored in the generalized knowledge distillation work. If the student only ever learns on teacher-generated text, there's a train-test mismatch: at inference time it's conditioning on its own mistakes, which it never saw during training. If instead you let the student generate its own reasoning and have the teacher score those tokens with its logits, the student gets corrected in exactly the states it actually visits. You can think of it as a cheap, dense form of RL, where the teacher's distribution acts like a per-token reward instead of one sparse "was the final answer right" signal at the end.

So my overall view is that RL with verifiable rewards is great but sparse, and sampled SFT is easy but lossy. Logits distillation, especially on-policy, sits in a sweet spot: dense, on-distribution feedback from a much stronger model. That's why I think it's one of the most promising ways to get small reasoning models to punch well above their weight. There are practical caveats, of course. You need access to the teacher's logits, and the student and teacher ideally share a tokenizer, though there's been progress on cross-tokenizer methods too.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly presents logits distillation, especially on-policy, as a promising way for small reasoning models to get closer to stronger teachers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest starting point is that most of the distillation people have been doing for reasoning models isn't really distillation in the classic Hinton sense. It's SFT on teacher traces. You sample a bunch of chains of thought from DeepSeek-R1 or whatever your big model is, you filter for correctness maybe, and then you train the small model to imitate those tokens. And that works remarkably well, which is sort of the surprising part, but it also throws away almost everything the teacher knows.

The way I think about it is: when the teacher emits a token, it has a full distribution over the vocabulary at that position. In a reasoning trace, that distribution is really informative. At a lot of positions the teacher is basically certain, it's just continuing an equation or whatever. But at the interesting positions, the places where you decide "wait, let me check this" or you pick which case to handle first or whether to backtrack, the teacher is actually hedging between several plausible continuations. Sampling one trace gives you a one-hot label at that spot. You've collapsed all of that uncertainty into a single arbitrary choice, and then you're penalizing the student for not matching that one arbitrary choice.

So logits distillation, or really matching the full distribution, gives you a much richer signal per token. You're not just saying "the answer was this token," you're saying "here's how plausible each alternative was." That matters a lot for small models because the thing they struggle with isn't producing fluent-looking reasoning, it's calibration. They'll confidently go down a wrong branch and never come back. If you can transfer the teacher's sense of "these three continuations were all reasonable here, this one was definitely not," you're transferring something closer to the search behavior rather than just the surface form of one search.

The other piece I'd emphasize is the data efficiency angle. Hard-label SFT on traces needs a lot of samples because each sample is giving you maybe a few bits of information at the critical positions. With soft targets you're getting a lot more bits per token, so you can get away with far fewer teacher samples, and compute on the teacher side is usually the expensive part for these long traces.

Now, the caveats. One is the capacity gap problem, which people have known about for a long time. If the teacher is way bigger than the student, trying to match its exact distribution can actually hurt, because the student just doesn't have the capacity to represent those modes and it ends up averaging them into mush. So you often want something like reverse KL, or some kind of on-policy variant where the student generates and you score with the teacher, rather than pure forward KL on teacher samples. That's where a lot of the actual recent gains come from, I think, more than the "logits versus tokens" distinction by itself.

The second caveat is tokenizer mismatch, which sounds boring but is a real blocker. If your teacher and student don't share a vocabulary, you can't just line up the logits. There are tricks for that, but it's friction, and it's part of why trace SFT became the default. Traces are tokenizer-agnostic. You can distill from an API.

But if you control both models, which the labs do, I think leaving the logits on the table is just wasteful. The teacher spent all this compute figuring out what it was uncertain about. Throwing that away and keeping only the argmax is kind of the worst compression of that knowledge you could pick.

r001.rationale: The response directly argues that logits distillation can give small reasoning models richer teacher signals and help them improve.

r002.rationale: It discusses calibration, search behavior, and the capacity gap, but does not suggest that strong reasoning depends more on effective inference-time compute than on parameter capacity.

astra-6.text:
I think the key intuition is that the teacher knows more than what shows up in a single sampled answer. When you distill on generated text, you’re showing the student one trajectory: these are the tokens the teacher chose. But the teacher’s logits also tell you which alternatives it considered plausible and how strongly it preferred one over another. That’s a much richer training signal.

For reasoning, that could help the student learn the local decisions that make a good reasoning trajectory—not just imitate the final answer. If several next steps are reasonable, you don’t necessarily want to train as though only the sampled one is correct.

Now, that doesn’t mean a small model can absorb everything a much larger teacher can do. Capacity still matters, and matching token distributions doesn’t automatically give you robust reasoning. But logits distillation could make the transfer more efficient, so you get closer to what the smaller model is actually capable of learning from its teacher.

r001.rationale: It says logits distillation could make transfer more efficient and help a smaller model get closer to what it can learn from a much larger teacher.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the intuition is that the teacher gives you much more information than just the answer it sampled. If you train on a reasoning trace, you see one path through the problem. But at every token, the teacher has a distribution over possible continuations. Logits distillation lets the student learn from that distribution, including alternatives that were plausible but weren’t selected.

That’s a richer learning signal. It tells the student not just what to do, but something about how strongly to prefer one continuation over another. And for reasoning, where small mistakes can compound over a long trajectory, learning those preferences could matter a lot.

The caveat is that the student still needs enough capacity, and it needs to learn what to do on the trajectories it actually visits. So I wouldn’t say logits distillation automatically closes the gap. But it could transfer substantially more of the teacher’s behavior than training only on its sampled outputs.

r001.rationale: It says logits distillation could transfer substantially more of a teacher’s behavior and help small reasoning models close the gap.
